lines.text: A vast land of rainforest and minerals, around one of the world's great rivers. This is the story of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
It begins with the river. Formed over a million years ago, the Congo is the deepest river in the world, crossing the equator twice.
Near its mouth rose the Kingdom of Kongo. Its kings took up Christianity from the Portuguese, and later fought the slave trade draining their people.
In the south-east, the Luba kingdom grew, known for its art of memory, carved boards that held its history.
In 1881 a trading post was set up on the river by the explorer Stanley. It would grow into Kinshasa, one of Africa's largest cities.
In 1885 King Leopold of Belgium claimed the Congo as his own private colony, the so-called Congo Free State.
Forced to gather rubber under terror, millions died. The outcry became the first great human rights campaign.
Mining began in the south, and today Congo supplies about seventy percent of the world's cobalt, much of it dug by hand.
In 1908 Belgium took the colony from Leopold. Its copper and uranium made Belgium rich, while the Congolese had few rights.
In Katanga, the mining town of Lubumbashi was founded, the capital of copper and cobalt.
Patrice Lumumba, born in 1925, would become the first prime minister of the free Congo.
That same year Virunga became Africa's first national park, home to volcanoes and some of the last mountain gorillas.
Mobutu, born in 1930, would become the army chief who ruled the country for more than thirty years.
Denis Mukwege, born in 1955, would become the doctor who treats women hurt in war, and win the Nobel Peace Prize.
Independence in 1960 brought chaos at once: mutiny, secession and outside powers. Lumumba was overthrown and killed within months.
Even so, a new nation was born, one of the largest in Africa, rich in forest, river and minerals.
And its music took off. Soukous, with its fast, bright guitars, spread across Africa from the sixties.
Felix Tshisekedi, born in 1963, would become the country's president in 2019.
In 1974, under Mobutu's Zaire, Kinshasa hosted the Rumble in the Jungle, where Muhammad Ali beat George Foreman with his rope-a-dope.
By the nineties Mobutu's rule was rotten. In 1996 a rebellion backed by neighbours swept across the country and drove him out.
Peace did not last. The Second Congo War drew in many nations and became the deadliest war since 1945.
In the east, the rebel group M23 took the city of Goma in 2012, and again in 2025.
And from 2018 an Ebola epidemic struck the eastern provinces, the second largest outbreak on record.
Rich in everything the world wants, the Congo is still waiting for the peace its people deserve.
